report.incident_title: Cost anomaly: Amazon EC2 - Compute, ap-south-1, usage type APS3-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes
report.summary: Confirmed by tool data: nginx-edge requests rose from 44k/day (2026-04-28) to 890k/day (2026-05-03) and fell to 190k by 05-05, and egress rose from 36 GB to 721 GB and back to 160 GB on the same curve, at roughly 0.8 MB per request on every day (E1, E2, E18). The AWS cost report shows the APS3-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes spike peaking at $74.80 on 05-03, totalling $205.53 (E23). On 05-03 the top-talkers summary attributes about 86% of requests to self-identified crawler user agents (GPTBot, Bytespider, ClaudeBot, meta-externalagent, Amazonbot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot), and about 52% of bytes to /static/js bundles (E25, E26). Crawlers touched about 1.9M distinct paths, most of which return 200 index.html via the try_files fallback (E27, E28). The log sample includes a 4.7 MB Bytespider download of a static JS file (E8). No deploy, config or infra change was recorded in the window (E20, E21). Assumptions and gaps: the top-talkers and per-byte breakdowns cover only 05-03, so the bot share on other days is unverified. The nginx config snapshot is dated 2026-05-06, so the caching and fallback settings in force on 04-29 are unconfirmed (E29). The robots.txt snapshot is for a different domain (E30). The cost report total of 205.53 differs from the stated 211.51 (E24). Blog, web-app and media-cdn have no metrics or logs, so the hypothesis that blog serves media directly from the host (H1) is refuted by the byte breakdown and unverified in full. What triggered the step-up on 04-29 is not identified.
report.root_cause: Mechanism supported by the evidence: AI and web crawlers, which self-identify as crawlers and come from cloud IP ranges, made a large increase in requests to nginx-edge starting 2026-04-29 (E1, E9, E25, E27). Because nginx-edge has no CDN in front and no rate limiting (E15, E28), every request reached the EC2 host and was served as full responses. Unknown paths return 200 index.html through the try_files fallback, and static JS and blog HTML were fetched repeatedly, so egress scaled with crawler request volume at about 0.8 MB per request (E18, E26, E8). The EC2 DataTransfer-Out cost followed that volume (E23). The initial trigger of the crawler increase was not identified, and the day-by-day match is only confirmed for 05-03.

hypotheses.statement: Spikes in AI and web crawler traffic (GPTBot, Bytespider, ClaudeBot, meta-externalagent, Amazonbot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot) scraped the site heavily—downloading index.html pages and static JS bundles (~0.8 MB per request)—driving ~86% of requests at peak and causing the EC2 egress cost surge.

corrective_actions.action: Reduce crawler load on nginx-edge now by rate-limiting or blocking the high-volume crawler user agents at nginx or the edge, after verifying their source IPs against published crawler ranges. Do not remove or weaken existing security controls to do this.
corrective_actions.rationale: Crawler requests account for about 86% of requests and most of the bytes on the peak day, so limiting them stops most of the egress growth quickly.

corrective_actions.action: Change the nginx location / try_files fallback so unknown paths return 404 instead of 200 index.html, which removes the cheap fake pages that crawlers index.
corrective_actions.rationale: Crawlers reached 1.9M distinct paths, and most of these are served as 200 index.html, which inflates crawl volume and bytes.

corrective_actions.action: Add daily alerts on nginx-edge requests and egress GB, and a per-user-agent request and byte breakdown, so a crawler surge is caught within a day. Also reconcile the cost report total against the incident figure.
corrective_actions.rationale: The anomaly ran about 7 days before detection, and the current metrics are daily only with no label breakdown.

corrective_actions.action: Put a CDN or caching layer in front of nginx-edge for static assets, and confirm the nginx config in force at the anomaly start before changing it.
corrective_actions.rationale: Static JS is already cacheable with immutable headers, but the absence of a CDN means cache hits do not reduce origin egress. The 2026-05-06 config snapshot does not confirm the 04-29 state.
